claim: Your morning coffee helped spark a revolution in the Caribbean.

knots.passage: Frenchman Gabriel de Clieu took a coffee plant to the French territory of Martinique in the Caribbean in the 1720s, from which much of the world's cultivated arabica coffee is descended. Coffee thrived in the climate and was conveyed across the Americas.
knots.hatnote: One French officer and a seedling, or so the story goes.

knots.passage: According to de Clieu's account, water was rationed on the voyage, and he shared his ration with the seedlings. The story is repeated in many histories of coffee. However, a recent history points out that though it may well be true that de Clieu brought a seedling to Martinique, and perhaps even that he shared his water ration with it, coffee was already growing in the Western Hemisphere: in the French colony of Saint-Domingue since 1715 and in the Dutch colony of Surinam since 1718.
knots.hatnote: The myth-check. A great story, but coffee had beaten him there.

knots.passage: Saint-Domingue became known as the "Pearl of the Antilles" – one of the richest colonies in the world in the 18th-century French empire. It was the greatest jewel in imperial France's mercantile crown. By the 1780s, Saint-Domingue produced about 40 percent of all the sugar and 60 percent of all the coffee consumed in Europe. By 1789, Saint Domingue was made up of about 8,000 plantations ..., producing one-half of all the sugar and coffee that was consumed in Europe and the Americas.
knots.hatnote: Saint-Domingue became the colony that grew most of Europe's coffee.

knots.passage: In 1791, Africans, who had been forced into bondage, and some Creoles took part in a Vodou ceremony at Bois Caïman and planned the Haitian Revolution.
knots.hatnote: The people forced to work those plantations planned a revolution.

payoff: By 1789, one colony grew half the coffee drunk in Europe and the Americas, and the people enslaved there rose up.
caveats: A darker hole: it ends in a slave revolution.

The hole now runs through Saint-Domingue (the old knot 3 looped back to the Coffee page). The Coffee page's sentence that plantation conditions "were a factor in the Haitian Revolution" is no longer a knot, because it couldn't be reached by a link.
